summary: Login slowness and 503s on auth-service (p99 ~90ms -> ~3.77s, 5xx ~0.2% -> ~14%) were caused by an inbound traffic surge that overwhelmed auth-service's fixed admission capacity, not by the bcrypt regression the reporter suspected. An ~3.8-3.9x traffic step starting in the 06:47-06:50 UTC buckets is visible at the api-gateway boundary and carried into auth-service as a stable ~37% subset; auth-service's worker pool filled (64/64, queues to 98763), the autoscaler could not exceed maxReplicas 8, and auth-service itself emitted "accept queue full" 503s. Confidence in H1 (capacity saturation) is 0.62 (medium); the mechanism and scope are well supported, with the residual uncertainty being whether the surge was genuine external demand or a client/retry storm (H5, 0.20) - both share the same mechanism and the same primary mitigation. All change-based causes were tested and excluded: no auth-service deployment in 25 hours, no bcrypt/log signature, redis-cache flat on all five metrics, and user-db connection growth follows rather than precedes onset.

ranked_hypotheses.title: Incoming login traffic surge overwhelms auth-service's fixed admission capacity (mechanism established; origin external/non-change-driven)
ranked_hypotheses.statement: Incoming request volume to the login path stepped up ~3.8-4.5x beginning in the 06:47-06:50 UTC buckets and auth-service could not absorb it. Its fixed worker pool (64/64) filled, the accept queue grew into the tens of thousands (peaks 98763), CPU pinned near 100%, and the autoscaler could not help because desired replicas (14) exceeded the configured maxReplicas (8). The saturated admission path itself returned 503, producing p99 ~3.8s and ~14% 5xx. This requires no auth-service code, config or resource change: no deployment or config change maps to onset (F1-F3, F16, F37-F40). The surge is not an auth-service-only internal echo — api-gateway request_rate rose ~3.9x on the identical bucket grid (F31, F32, F33) and the gateway's own error_rate reached only ~half of auth-service's, consistent with auth-service originating the 5xx (F35). The remaining open question is the surge's origin (external demand vs client loop), treated separately in H5.

causal_chain.claim: Inbound request volume steps ~3.8x starting in the 06:47-06:50 buckets: auth-service 394 -> ~1.49k req/s and api-gateway ~1.2k -> 4.79k req/s on the identical bucket grid
auth-service rate is a stable ~37% subset of the gateway's volume throughout, so this is not a multiplied internal echo contained inside auth-service
auth-service worker pool saturates (active=64/64, queue 39035, peaks 98763) with CPU pinned ~100%
The autoscaler cannot relieve pressure: desired 14 replicas > maxReplicas 8, so no scale-out occurs
auth-service itself rejects requests at admission with 'accept queue full' 503s on POST /v1/auth/login; its own logs show no bcrypt/hash errors and zero downstream timeout/DB errors
Resulting symptom: p99 jumps from ~90ms to ~3.77s and 5xx rises from 0.2% to ~13.8-14.1%
The gateway's error_rate rises only to ~6-9% (~half of auth-service's ~14%), indicating the 5xx originate at auth-service rather than at the gateway
No service outside the gateway->auth-service path degrades: pricing-engine, market-data-service, portfolio-service request_rate/latency_p99/error_rate are flat through 06:47-06:52

assumptions: maxReplicas 8 and worker-pool size 64 were the values in force at onset; both are known only from F12's autoscaler warning text and report text, and no restart/replica-count series exists to confirm them at pod level

The request_rate series reflects inbound load reaching auth-service; the gateway has no retries/upstream-5xx counter or client/endpoint attribution, so demand-driven surge vs retry storm cannot be separated from these series (F36, F43)

ranked_hypotheses.title: Retry loop / client storm amplifies traffic into the login path (shared multiplier), saturating auth-service
ranked_hypotheses.statement: Rather than genuine new demand, a misbehaving client, client-side retry loop, or upstream retry amplification multiplied request volume entering through api-gateway and terminating at auth-service's /v1/auth/login, overwhelming auth-service's fixed admission capacity (the H1 mechanism). This is a genuinely different ORIGIN than H1: no new external demand, just multiplied retries. It matters because the fix differs — block the offending client / fix the retry loop rather than raise maxReplicas. The findings cannot confirm this: the gateway exposes no client/IP attribution, no per-route request rate, and no retries or upstream-5xx counter (F36, F43), and the ~37% auth-service-to-gateway ratio (F33) is consistent with a shared multiplier scaling both series proportionally.

causal_chain.claim: A client/upstream retry multiplier inflates volume at the gateway boundary, driving both gateway and auth-service request_rate up proportionally
auth-service's rate remains a stable ~37% subset of the gateway's, consistent with a shared retry multiplier as well as with genuine demand
The amplified volume saturates auth-service's fixed worker pool and accepted-queue, yielding 'accept queue full' 503s and p99 ~3.8s

assumptions: A retry loop would still produce the observed monotone, ~8-bucket ramp; F44's smooth multi-bucket buildup is more consistent with building demand than an instantaneous client-triggered jump, which weakens but does not eliminate a gradually worsening retry loop
A retry-driven surge would be expected to leave a gateway retry/upstream-5xx signature, but no such counter exists (F43) so neither confirmation nor refutation is possible

ranked_hypotheses.title: user-db connection-pool / query pressure is the first mover and slows auth-service logins
ranked_hypotheses.statement: user-db slowed (connection or query-latency pressure) at onset, so each auth-service login blocked on the DB, holding worker slots and producing queue saturation, 503s and p99 ~3.8s.

causal_chain.claim: user-db connections_active steps ~3x from ~24-26 to ~72-82 in the 06:52 UTC one-minute bucket
user-db query latency / pool wait rises, so auth-service logins block on DB calls and hold worker slots
Queue backlog yields 503 accept-queue rejections and p99 ~3.8s

assumptions: user-db exposes no connection-wait or pool-saturation series (F30), so a DB-side admission bottleneck cannot be directly measured or fully excluded
ranked_hypotheses.rejection_reason: DB-side slowdown mechanism unsupported and timing is backwards: the connection step is at 06:52 (F26) while the auth-service traffic surge begins in the 06:47-06:48 bucket (F16, F29), so DB connection growth follows rather than precedes the load step and reads as an effect of the surge. user-db cpu_pct is flat 16-20% including onset buckets (F17), slow_queries_per_min is flat 0.18-0.51 with no step (F27), and replication_lag_ms is flat ~27.6-32.3ms (F28) — no query-latency, storage or replication fault. auth-service logged zero DB/timeout errors (F15). Residual: no connection-wait metric exists (F30), which caps confidence but does not re-rank this above H1.

ranked_hypotheses.title: Shared redis-cache (co-tenant) degradation propagates into auth-service login path
ranked_hypotheses.statement: The shared redis-cache used by auth-service, portfolio-service, pricing-engine and market-data-service degraded (e.g. eviction / hit-ratio / memory pressure driven by the 05:50 portfolio-service 'Holdings export' release), slowing session/token lookups inside logins and backing up auth-service's workers.

causal_chain.claim: portfolio-service v4.4.0 dep-5803 (CSV 'Holdings export') at 05:50 adds load to the shared redis-cache
redis-cache degrades in a way that slows auth-service session/token lookups
slower logins back up auth-service workers, producing queue saturation and 503s

assumptions: A tenant-scoped (auth-service keyspace / connection pool) effect invisible in whole-instance aggregates could still exist; redis-cache exposes no per-tenant breakdown and no redis logs were retrieved
ranked_hypotheses.rejection_reason: Directly tested and refuted at the aggregate level: all five redis-cache indicators are indistinguishable from baseline across the 06:47-06:54 onset interval — cpu_pct flat 20.6-25.6% (F18/F24), hit_ratio_pct flat 94.4-97.4% with no miss collapse (F20), evictions_per_min flat 1.17-4.42 keys/min with no storm (F21), memory_pct flat 64.5-76.3% never near a limit (F22), connected_clients steady ~286-337 with no reconnect storm (F23); check was complete (41/41 points, missing_points 0) so the absence is not a truncation artifact (F25). This also refutes the HIST-107 cold-cache-storm shape (F7). Co-tenant check negative: portfolio-service latency_p99 flat ~174-203ms (F49/F50). Residual: a tenant-scoped effect invisible to aggregate metrics; data-source limitation is permanent.

ranked_hypotheses.title: Reported auth-service code/config regression (bcrypt cost bump) after an auth-service release — reporter's suspicion
ranked_hypotheses.statement: An undocumented or out-of-band auth-service change raised a CPU-heavy synchronous path (e.g. bcrypt cost factor), inflating per-request CPU work so each login takes seconds and the worker pool backs up. This mirrors HIST-101 (bcrypt cost 10->14, rolled back).

causal_chain.claim: An auth-service release or out-of-band artifact change shipped a costlier password-hash / slow path
Per-request CPU cost rises so 64 workers each hold their slot for seconds, backlogging the queue
Queue/accept backlog produces 503s and p99 ~3.8s on /v1/auth/login

assumptions: A deployment or image-digest change exists that the deployment API did not return; no artifact/image-digest/hash surface is exposed anywhere (F41), so this is excluded only inferentially
ranked_hypotheses.rejection_reason: No auth-service deployment exists anywhere in the 25h pre-onset window (F1, F2, F39); the only deployment in the span is portfolio-service v4.4.0 (F1, F38). The only config change is cfg-2801 log.level INFO->WARN (F3, F37, F40). No bcrypt/hash/verify error signature appears in the logs (F14); the observed failure is admission-queue rejection (F10) rather than slow hashing (F19); and no artifact/image-digest/hash-change record exists in any change stream (F41). Its only support is a same-shaped past incident (F6) plus the reporter's prior. Residual: an out-of-band artifact swap is excluded only by absence-of-record/inference, not by direct artifact evidence.

facts.statement: auth-service p99 latency was ~88-92ms through 06:51 UTC, then jumped to ~3.77s in the 06:54 bucket and stayed ~3.7-3.9s through 08:59, placing onset between 06:51 and 06:54 UTC.
auth-service HTTP 5xx error_rate was ~0.2% up to 06:40 UTC, then 7.11% in the 06:50-07:00 bucket and steady ~13.8-14.1% thereafter, matching the reported 503 symptom.
The 503s are generated BY auth-service, not propagated: its own ERROR logs read 'request rejected: accept queue full, returning 503 (POST /v1/auth/login)', 372 occurrences, first_seen 06:55:42 UTC.

auth-service worker pool saturation precedes the 503s: WARN 'worker pool saturated (active=64/64, queue=39035)' first seen 06:54:53 UTC, 249 occurrences, queues reaching 98763, with CPU pinned near 100% (97.38% avg in the 07:00 bucket).

auth-service could not scale out: WARN 'autoscaler: desired replicas 14 exceeds maxReplicas 8; cannot scale further' first at 06:57:15 UTC (34 occurrences), while incoming request_rate rose ~3.8x from ~394 req/s to ~1.49k req/s.

auth-service request_rate sat at ~391-404 req/s through the 06:36 bucket, then the 06:47 bucket shows avg 765.13 / max 1425.56 and the 06:58 bucket 1528.72, so the traffic step begins in the 06:47 bucket immediately before the ~06:54 worker-pool saturation.
api-gateway request_rate rose from a flat ~1,180-1,325 req/s baseline through the 06:48 bucket to 4,790 req/s in the 06:58 bucket (~3.9x) on the same bucket grid in which auth-service's rate rose.

auth-service request_rate rose on the identical bucket grid from a flat ~383-418 req/s baseline through 06:48 to avg 1749.75 at 06:58; both services first clearly exceed baseline in the 06:50 bucket, so the gateway is not flat while auth-service rises.

api-gateway request_rate shows a smooth, monotone ramp building across ~8 one-minute buckets (06:40-06:50 flat ~1178-1348, then 06:51 1652.95 through 07:04 5197.35) rather than one instantaneous client-triggered jump.
api-gateway p99 latency stepped from a flat ~201-226ms baseline (through 06:53) to 4024.51ms at 06:54 and stayed 3648-4200ms through 07:05, coinciding exactly with auth-service's onset.

api-gateway's own error_rate stayed ~0.13-0.27% through the 06:51 bucket, then jumped to avg 6.23% (max 9.4) at 06:54 and 9.09% at 06:57 - only about half of auth-service's ~13.8-14.1%, indicating the 5xx originate at auth-service and are only partially reflected at the gateway.

No auth-service deployment exists anywhere in the 25-hour pre-onset window: auth-service deployments queried back to 2026-04-21T06:00Z return count=0, and all-services deployments over the extended 25-hour window return exactly one entry, dep-5803 portfolio-service v4.4.0 at 2026-04-22T05:50:00Z.

The only config change in the 33-hour widened all-services window is cfg-2801, auth-service 'log.level' INFO->WARN at 2026-04-22T03:40:00Z by config-bot ('Reduce log volume') - a logging verbosity change, not a bcrypt/resource/limit change.

auth-service logs contain no bcrypt/hash/password-verify error signature; all 657 WARN/ERROR lines in 06:00-08:59 are limited to 5 patterns, the only ERROR being 'accept queue full' 503s (372) and the top WARN 'worker pool saturated' (249).

auth-service produced zero dependency/connection-timeout log lines: 'timeout' search returned total_matched=0 and 'db' (WARN+) returned total_matched=0 across 06:00-08:59, so the failure is local accept-queue rejection, not downstream-timeout-driven.
user-db cpu_pct is flat ~16-20% across the whole 05:30-08:59 range (max 19.99, mean 18.0), including the 06:47-06:58 buckets (17.76), so the DB is not the CPU-bound source of the latency.

user-db slow_queries_per_min is flat across the whole 06:30-07:10 window with no step at or near the connection jump (values ~0.18-0.51, mean 0.31), so query latency did not step before or with the connection growth.
user-db replication_lag_ms is flat ~27.6-32.3ms (mean 29.98) for every one-minute bucket 06:30-07:10, so the DB's storage/replication layer shows no fault.
user-db connections_active stepped sharply between the 06:51 and 06:52 buckets (flat ~23.4-26.5 through 06:51, then avg 72.59 at 06:52), a discrete ~3x step in the 06:52 one-minute bucket.

Comparison of onset timestamps: the user-db connection step is at ~06:52 UTC while the auth-service traffic surge begins in the 06:47-06:48 bucket, so the connection step follows the traffic surge by ~4-5 minutes and is an effect, not the first mover.

All five redis-cache indicators are flat across the 06:47-06:54 onset interval: hit_ratio_pct mean 96.10% (min 94.44, max 97.40) with no step, evictions_per_min oscillating 1.17-4.42 with no storm, memory_pct mean 69.98% (range 64.49-76.30) never near a limit, connected_clients steady ~286-337 with no reconnect storm, and cpu_pct flat 20.59-25.59%.
Cross-service sweep 06:30-07:10 UTC shows no traffic step at 06:47-06:52 for pricing-engine (flat 587-687 req/s), market-data-service (flat 864-1025 req/s), or portfolio-service (flat 523-618 req/s).

Peer latency_p99 is flat straight through the 06:47-06:54 onset window (pricing-engine 55.94-65.16ms, market-data-service 35.67-42.56ms, portfolio-service 164.72-194.13ms), and peer error_rate stays flat and low (pricing-engine 0.10-0.32%, market-data-service 0.10-0.31%), so there is no latency or error blast radius outside auth-service.

Among the services sharing the api-gateway ingress, the traffic step is present only on api-gateway and auth-service, both rising on the identical 120s bucket grid from the 06:50 bucket; the other services are statistically indistinguishable from baseline, so blast radius is auth-service-only.

api-gateway exposes no client/endpoint-level metric or log attribution (available_metrics only cpu_pct, error_rate, latency_p99_ms, memory_pct, request_rate, restarts; the only log patterns are routine heartbeats), so the surge cannot be attributed to specific clients or to the /v1/auth/login endpoint from gateway telemetry.

api-gateway logs at 06:40-07:05 contain zero error-level entries and only routine INFO patterns ('connection pool stats: healthy', 'config reloaded (no changes)'), with no retry, throttle, upstream-5xx, or client-attribution line anywhere in the window.

The evidence localises the surge to traffic entering through api-gateway and terminating at auth-service rather than being generated internally by auth-service, but does not identify which client or endpoint emitted it.

Prior precedent HIST-101 ('bcrypt cost factor raised 10->14 in release v6.4.0', rolled back) matches the reported latency+503 symptom pair and is the source of the reporter's suspicion, but none of its mechanism appears in this incident's change record.

No artifact/container-identity change surface has evidence for auth-service: the dependency graph exposes no image-digest, binary-hash or pod-revision node, and no image/artifact change record appears in any queried change stream.

assumptions: maxReplicas 8 and worker-pool size 64 were the values in force at onset; both are known only from the autoscaler warning text (F12) and the incident report, and no restart/pod-count/replica series exists to confirm them at pod level (no such metric surfaced).

The request_rate series reflects inbound load reaching auth-service and api-gateway; the gateway has no retries/upstream-5xx counter or client/endpoint attribution, so a demand-driven surge vs a retry storm cannot be fully separated from these series (F36, F43, F46).

The traffic step visible at the gateway is genuinely upstream of auth-service and not a metric-collection artifact; the two services' onsets coincide on the same bucket grid (F31, F32) and their ratio is a stable ~37% (F33, F47).

The absence of an out-of-band artifact/image-digest change for auth-service is an absence-of-record: no image-digest, binary-hash, or pod-revision surface is exposed anywhere, so H2's out-of-band path is excluded inferentially rather than by direct artifact evidence (F41).

The user-db connection growth at 06:52 is a consequence of the auth-service traffic surge (pool usage from more concurrent logins), not an independent DB-side first mover; this is supported by timing and by flat slow-queries/replication lag, but no connection-wait or pool-saturation metric exists to measure it directly (F26, F27, F28, F30).

Whole-instance redis-cache aggregates are the right level to judge H3: a degradation isolated to auth-service's own keyspace or connection pool could in principle be masked by healthy aggregates (F5, F18).
kyc-provider is external with has_telemetry:false, so it is assumed not to be a contributor on the basis of no evidence rather than positive health data (F4).

(demoted from facts: no verified observation backs it) auth-service's request rate is a stable ~37% fraction of the gateway's throughout, consistent with auth-service traffic being a subset of genuine gateway inbound traffic rather than an amplified internal echo.

(demoted from facts: no verified observation backs it) Interpretation of the signature: the failure mode is classic accept-queue/worker-pool saturation under a load spike with a too-low replica cap, not slow synchronous password hashing; a bcrypt cost bump would show uniformly slow hash work with CPU pegged and no accept-queue rejection messages.

(demoted from facts: no verified observation backs it) The direct test of the H3 redis-cache hop is complete (partial:false, missing_points:0, 41/41 points at 60s buckets), so the absence of a cache-pressure signature in the onset window is not a truncation artifact.

timeline.event: Sole config change in the 33-hour window: cfg-2801, auth-service 'log.level' INFO->WARN by config-bot ('Reduce log volume') - a logging change, not a resource/bcrypt change.
Sole deployment in the 25-hour window: dep-5803 portfolio-service v4.4.0 'Holdings export' (status live, not rolled back). No auth-service deployment exists anywhere in the span.
Baseline holds across the ingress: api-gateway ~1,178-1,348 req/s, auth-service ~391-404 req/s, redis-cache all five metrics flat, peer services flat.

Traffic surge begins: auth-service request_rate steps to avg 765.13 / max 1425.56 in the 06:47 bucket (from ~391-404), and the api-gateway rate ramp starts on the same grid. No change timestamp maps to onset.
Both api-gateway (1500.82) and auth-service (452.43) first clearly exceed baseline on the identical 120s bucket grid; peer services show no step.
auth-service p99 latency is still ~88-92ms and error_rate still ~0.2% - the last pre-onset minute.

user-db connections_active steps ~3x (from flat ~23.4-26.5 to avg 72.59) - ~4-5 minutes AFTER the traffic surge began, so it is an effect, not the first mover. slow_queries and replication lag remain flat.
auth-service p99 jumps to ~3.77s and the gateway p99 steps from ~211ms to 4024.51ms; redis-cache metrics still show no step across all five indicators.
auth-service worker pool saturates: WARN 'worker pool saturated (active=64/64, queue=39035)' first seen, 249 occurrences, queues reaching 98763; CPU pinned near 100%.
auth-service begins emitting its own 503s: ERROR 'request rejected: accept queue full, returning 503 (POST /v1/auth/login)', 372 occurrences.
Autoscaler ceiling hit: WARN 'autoscaler: desired replicas 14 exceeds maxReplicas 8; cannot scale further' (34 occurrences). Incoming request_rate up ~3.8x from ~394 to ~1.49k req/s.
Peak of the surge on the observed grid: gateway 4,790-5,197 req/s, auth-service ~1,749.75 req/s; gateway error_rate 9.09% vs auth-service ~13.8-14.1%.
auth-service p99 remains ~3.7-3.9s and 5xx ~14%; no dependency/connection-timeout log lines appear anywhere in 06:00-08:59.

recommended_actions.action: Raise auth-service maxReplicas (the configured ceiling of 8 reported by the autoscaler) so the autoscaler can reach its desired replica count of 14; this is the exact setting that prevented scale-out at 06:57:15 UTC.
recommended_actions.rationale: The autoscaler computed desired replicas 14 but was blocked by maxReplicas 8 while the worker pool sat at 64/64 with queues to 98763 (F11, F12). Lifting the cap directly restores admission capacity and is the primary mitigation regardless of whether the surge is genuine demand or a retry storm.

recommended_actions.action: Increase auth-service admission capacity per replica (worker pool size above 64) and/or front the login path with queue-depth-based shedding/backpressure rather than accepting unbounded queue growth, then verify p99 and 5xx recover as load continues.
recommended_actions.rationale: The failure is admission-bound at the accept queue, so raising the per-replica concurrency and bounding the queue converts overload into fast, controlled rejections instead of 3.8s latency from 98763-deep queues (F11, F10, F8).

recommended_actions.action: Instrument and preserve gateway-side attribution before the next occurrence: add per-client/IP request counts, per-route request rate, and retries / upstream-5xx counters at api-gateway, and retain client attribution in gateway logs. These surfaces do not currently exist (request_rate_by_client, request_rate_by_route, retries_per_sec, upstream_5xx all returned not_found).
recommended_actions.rationale: The single unresolved question - genuine external demand (H1) vs a client/retry storm (H5) - is unanswerable today because the decisive series are absent (F36, F43, F46). Both origins share the mechanism and the primary fix, but they imply different follow-on remediation (block/repair the offending client vs permanent capacity sizing).

recommended_actions.action: Size auth-service capacity to the observed surge envelope (~4x baseline on the login path, sustained for over 2 hours) and add load-based alerting on worker-pool occupancy and accept-queue depth so saturation is detected before p99 crosses the SLO.
recommended_actions.rationale: auth-service request_rate rose ~3.8-4.5x (F16, F32) and p99/5xx stayed degraded from ~06:54 through 08:59 (F8, F9), so the current fixed capacity is undersized for reachable demand; earlier detection at 06:54:53 (worker pool saturated) would have given ~40 minutes of warning before the peak.

recommended_actions.action: If gateway attribution shows a dominant single client or a retry signature once instrumented, block or rate-limit that client at the gateway and fix the responsible retry loop; keep the capacity fix in place either way.
recommended_actions.rationale: H5 (retry loop / client storm, 0.20) shares H1's mechanism but has a different remedy; the decisive evidence is obtainable once per-client and retries/upstream-5xx telemetry exists at the gateway (F36, F43). The smooth ~8-bucket monotone ramp (F44) is more consistent with building demand than an instantaneous client-triggered jump, which weakens but does not exclude H5.

recommended_actions.action: Add per-tenant (per-caller) redis-cache breakdown for the shared instance, and a pod-level worker/hash-timing and image-digest/pod-revision surface for auth-service, so future co-tenant cache effects and out-of-band artifact changes are detectable rather than only excludable by absence of record.
recommended_actions.rationale: redis-cache exposes only whole-instance aggregates, so a keyspace-scoped degradation for auth-service would be masked by healthy aggregates (F5, F18); and no image-digest/pod-revision surface exists, so H2's out-of-band path is excluded only inferentially (F41).

recommended_actions.action: Adopt a login-path playbook that distinguishes admission saturation from slow-work regressions before invoking past-incident precedent: check for accept-queue/worker-pool saturation messages and autoscaler ceiling warnings first, and treat HIST-101's bcrypt signature as requiring positive artifact evidence.
recommended_actions.rationale: The reporter's prior was driven by the same-shaped HIST-101 (F6), but this incident's change record contains no auth-service release in 25 hours and no bcrypt signature; the observable difference (accept-queue rejection vs uniformly slow hashing) is now documented in F19/F14.

data_gaps: The origin of the ~3.8-3.9x surge is unidentified: no per-client, per-route, retries, or upstream-5xx series exists at api-gateway (all four queries returned not_found), and gateway logs carry no client/endpoint attribution. This is a permanent data-source limitation, not a missing query, and it is the single reason H1 (genuine demand) and H5 (client/retry storm) cannot be separated - though both share the same mechanism and primary fix.

No artifact/image-digest/pod-revision surface exists in any queried change stream or dependency node, so an out-of-band auth-service image swap or rolling pod replacement cannot be positively ruled out - only that no deploy or bcrypt-cost change is recorded (auth-service deployments count 0 over 25 hours).

user-db exposes no connection-wait or pool-saturation metric and no true query p99 latency, so a DB-side admission bottleneck cannot be directly measured; only connections_active and slow_queries_per_min were available as proxies.

redis-cache telemetry is whole-instance aggregate only; no per-tenant breakdown exists, and no redis-cache logs were retrieved, so an effect scoped to auth-service's own keyspace is invisible to the aggregate-level refutation.

The incident report's claimed 'auth-service release' has no counterpart in the deployment record (count 0 across 25 hours), and no release-notes-level detail (bcrypt cost values, resource limits) exists for any service, so the report's premise could not be verified directly.

Peer-side WARN+/ERROR logs for pricing-engine and market-data-service during 06:30-07:10 could not be retrieved (budget_exhausted), so peer 'healthy' calls rest on metrics (request_rate, latency_p99, error_rate) rather than log confirmation; market-data-service cpu_pct and portfolio-service error_rate were also not retrieved.

No pod/node-level CPU, memory, or threadpool metrics for auth-service hosts were obtainable, so the saturation could not be decomposed further than service-level cpu_pct plus the log-embedded worker-pool queue evidence.
what_would_change_the_conclusion: Gateway-side telemetry showing a single client or IP dominating the ~3.9x step (or a retries/upstream-5xx counter with amplification) would move the conclusion from H1's genuine external demand toward H5's retry loop / client storm - changing the primary remediation to blocking the offending client rather than capacity sizing.
Per-route gateway data showing the surge concentrated on /v1/auth/login rather than spread across gateway routes would strengthen H5 or a login-targeted flood over broad demand.
Evidence of a recorded or out-of-band auth-service artifact change (image digest, binary hash, or pod revision differing from baseline) would revive H2, notwithstanding the empty deployment record.
A redis-cache per-tenant series showing a step in auth-service's own keyspace (or cache-miss collapse scoped to auth-service) during 06:47-06:54 would revive H3 despite the flat aggregate metrics.
A user-db connection-wait or pool-saturation series (or a true query-latency p99) stepping BEFORE 06:47 would revive H4 and reverse the current direction-of-causality finding.

Evidence that the auth-service request_rate series was a collection artifact or that no new load reached the login path at all (e.g. the rate rise was internal amplification) would undermine H1's mechanism.

findings.statement: Across ALL services in 05:00-09:00 on 2026-04-22 there was exactly ONE deployment: dep-5803 portfolio-service v4.4.0 'Holdings export' (CSV export endpoint) at 2026-04-22T05:50:00Z, status 'live', rolled_back_at null. No auth-service deployment occurred in this window.

No auth-service release was found when querying auth-service deployments back to 02:00 (count 0), so the reported 'auth-service release' in this incident is not present in the deployment record; no bcrypt cost / auth-library / resource-limit change appears anywhere in the 02:00-09:00 deployment data.

Config changes across ALL services in 05:00-09:00 = 0 (count 0, empty list). Widening to auth-service for 2026-04-21T09:00Z-2026-04-22T09:00Z returned only one change: cfg-2801, auth-service 'log.level' INFO->WARN at 2026-04-22T03:40:00Z by config-bot ('Reduce log volume') -- a logging verbosity change, not a bcrypt/resource/limit change.

auth-service dependency map (both directions): upstream caller api-gateway -> auth-service (http); downstream from auth-service: user-db (postgres, kind db), redis-cache (redis, kind cache), kyc-provider (external, has_telemetry false). redis-cache is flagged shared:true; user-db and kyc-provider are not shared.

SHARED COMPONENT: redis-cache is a shared cache consumed by four independent services -- auth-service, portfolio-service, pricing-engine, market-data-service -- all with kind 'cache'. So a redis-cache degradation or a cache-pressure event driven by the OTHER tenants (e.g. the 05:50 portfolio-service v4.4.0 'Holdings export' release) can reach auth-service's login path through this shared dependency.

Prior 'bcrypt regression' precedent = HIST-101 (2025-08-14, 'Login latency after auth-service release', services [auth-service], symptoms 'login p99 4s','503 on login','high cpu'): root cause 'bcrypt cost factor raised 10->14 in release v6.4.0', category bad_deployment, resolution 'Rolled back v6.4.0'. Owned by auth-service. Nearest other login-path precedents: HIST-109 (2025-07-11, JWT library upgrade changed clock-skew default; 401 invalid_token) and HIST-108 (2025-10-01, JWT key rotation published new key before all pods loaded JWKS; 401 invalid_token) -- both auth-service, both rolled back/pinned. Only HIST-101 matches the latency+503 symptom pair.

findings.statement: auth-service p99 latency was ~88-92ms through 06:51 UTC, then jumped to ~3.77s in the 06:54 bucket and stayed at ~3.7-3.9s through 08:59. Onset therefore falls between 06:51 and 06:54 UTC (3-minute buckets).
auth-service error_rate (HTTP 5xx) was ~0.2% up to 06:40 UTC, then 7.11% in the 06:50-07:00 bucket and steady ~13.8-14.1% thereafter, matching the reported 503 symptom.
The 503s are generated BY auth-service, not propagated: its own ERROR logs read 'request rejected: accept queue full, returning 503 (POST /v1/auth/login)', 372 occurrences, first_seen 06:55:42 UTC.

refs.quote: request rejected: accept queue full, returning 503 (POST /v1/auth/login)

findings.statement: auth-service worker pool saturation precedes the 503s: WARN 'worker pool saturated (active=64/64, queue=39035)' first seen 06:54:53 UTC, 249 occurrences; queues reach 98763. CPU is pinned near 100% (97.38% avg in the 07:00 bucket).

auth-service cannot scale out of the saturation: WARN 'autoscaler: desired replicas 14 exceeds maxReplicas 8; cannot scale further' first at 06:57:15 UTC (34 occurrences), while incoming request_rate rose ~3.8x from ~394 req/s to ~1.49k req/s.

findings.statement: user-db shows concurrent, not-cause-identified movement: connections_active rose from ~24-25 (06:00-06:30) to avg 79.3/max 84.53 in the 07:00 bucket, while user-db cpu_pct stayed flat at ~18% all window.

auth-service logs contain NO bcrypt/hash/password-verify error signature; all 657 WARN/ERROR lines in 06:00-08:59 are limited to 5 patterns, of which the only ERROR pattern is 'request rejected: accept queue full, returning 503 (POST /v1/auth/login)' (372) and the top WARN is 'worker pool saturated (active=64/64, queue=...)' (249). The only non-load warnings in the window are 'slow request 3759ms on /internal/metrics' (1, at 06:19:11) and 'clock drift ... resyncing with NTP' (1, 07:29:32).

findings.statement: auth-service produced zero dependency/connection-timeout log lines: a search for 'timeout' returned total_matched=0 and a search for 'db' (WARN+) returned total_matched=0 across 06:00-08:59, so there is no logged evidence of DB or session-store connection errors — the failure is local accept-queue rejection, not downstream-timeout-driven.

The change timeline vs onset: the sole window deployment is portfolio-service v4.4.0 dep-5803 at 05:50 UTC and it is unrelated to auth; the sole config change, cfg-2801 auth-service log.level INFO->WARN at 03:40 UTC, is a logging change. Meanwhile auth-service request_rate sat at ~391-404 req/s through the 06:36 bucket, then the 06:47 bucket shows avg 765.13 / max 1425.56 and the 06:58 bucket 1528.72 — the surge begins in the 06:47 bucket, immediately before the ~06:54 worker-pool saturation. No change timestamp maps to onset; the traffic step does.

user-db shows no infra fault that precedes onset: cpu_pct is flat ~16-20% across the whole 05:30-08:59 range (max 19.99, mean 18.0), including the 06:47-06:58 buckets (17.76) that bracket onset, so the DB is not the CPU-bound source of the latency. user-db's own available metrics are cpu_pct, connections_active, disk_used_pct, replication_lag_ms, slow_queries_per_min.

The SHARED dependency redis-cache is healthy and flat through the window: cpu_pct never leaves ~21-23% (min 19.51, max 25.59, mean 22.02) with no step at onset, and redis-cache exposes no anomaly (available_metrics: connected_clients, cpu_pct, evictions_per_min, hit_ratio_pct, memory_pct). Likewise portfolio-service (the only deployer, and a redis-cache co-tenant) shows flat latency_p99 ~174-203ms across 05:30-08:59 — no co-tenant blast radius.

Interpretation of the signature: auth-service's failure mode is classic accept-queue/worker-pool saturation under a load spike with a too-low replica cap ('autoscaler: desired replicas 14 exceeds maxReplicas 8', first 06:57:15) — accept-queue full, queue depth into the tens of thousands — not slow synchronous password hashing. A bcrypt cost bump would manifest as uniformly slow hash work with CPU pegged and no accept-queue rejection messages; the observed messages are admission-control/queue rejections. This signature matches load/capacity saturation rather than HIST-101's bcrypt-regression pattern, and matches no downstream error pattern (no timeouts, no DB errors).

refs.quote: request rejected: accept queue full, returning 503 (POST /v1/auth/login)
autoscaler: desired replicas <n> exceeds maxReplicas <n>; cannot scale further

findings.statement: redis-cache hit_ratio_pct is flat across 06:30-07:10 at fine (60s) resolution: mean 96.10%, min 94.44%, max 97.40%, with no step at 06:47-06:54. Baseline minutes 06:30-06:46 average ~96.1-97.4 (e.g. 06:30 97.06, 06:40 95.20, 06:46 96.30) and the onset minutes are the same band (06:54 96.14, 06:55 96.04, 06:56 94.44, 06:57 95.39). There is no hit-ratio collapse (no mass-miss event) at onset.

redis-cache evictions_per_min shows no step at 06:47-06:54: the whole 06:30-07:10 window oscillates in a narrow 1.17-4.42 keys/min band (mean 2.91), with pre-onset values 06:42 1.17, 06:46 2.31, 06:47 3.21 and onset values 06:54 4.42, 06:55 1.97, 06:56 3.49 — the 4.42 max at 06:54 is within the same noise band seen later (07:01 4.32). No eviction storm or memory-pressure-driven eviction burst occurs.

redis-cache memory_pct is flat and NOT near a limit: mean 69.98%, range 64.49-76.30% across 06:30-07:10, with pre-onset 06:46 72.79 and onset 06:47 76.30 / 06:54 73.25, i.e. the single highest value (76.30) is a one-minute blip immediately before the 06:54 saturation and is not sustained. There is no memory exhaustion signature to force evictions.

redis-cache connected_clients shows no step at onset: a steady ~286-337 clients across the whole window (mean 310.34), pre-onset 06:46 336.28, onset 06:54 296.73 / 06:55 320.43 / 06:57 312.55. Connection count neither drops (client disconnect/failover) nor spikes (connection storm) at 06:47-06:54. This contradicts the HIST-107 'cold cache storm after redis failover' shape (which would show a client-reconnect storm and hit-ratio collapse).

redis-cache cpu_pct referenced against the same window also shows no step: 60s-resolution values stay in 20.59-25.59% (mean 22.17), pre-onset 06:47 22.92, onset 06:54 22.56 / 06:57 21.32. So all four cache-pressure indicators (evictions, hit_ratio, connected_clients, memory) plus cpu_pct are flat/unchanged across 06:47-06:54.

Direct test of the H3 hop: redis-cache exposes NO cache-pressure signature (eviction, miss/hit-ratio, memory, client-count) that steps in the 06:47-06:54 onset interval; all five available metrics (connected_clients, cpu_pct, evictions_per_min, hit_ratio_pct, memory_pct) are statistically indistinguishable from the 06:30-06:46 baseline. The result is complete (partial:false, missing_points:0, 41/41 points at 60s buckets), so this absence is not an artifact of truncation. H3's cache-degradation mechanism is not supported by redis-cache's own telemetry in the onset window.

user-db connections_active stepped sharply between the 06:51 and 06:52 UTC buckets: it was flat ~23.4-26.5 through 06:51 (06:44 avg 25.29, 06:45 26.51, 06:46 25.26, 06:47 24.78, 06:48 24.46, 06:49 23.39, 06:50 25.84, 06:51 26.39) and then jumped to avg 72.59 at 06:52, 74.03 at 06:53, 79.84 at 06:54, 78.36 at 06:55, 81.93 at 06:56. This is a discrete ~3x step, not a ramp, with onset in the 06:52 UTC one-minute bucket (bucket_seconds=60, 13 points, partial=false).

user-db slow_queries_per_min is FLAT across the whole 06:30-07:10 window and shows NO step at or near the connection jump: values stay in ~0.18-0.51 (mean 0.31, min 0.18, max 0.51), with 06:50=0.29, 06:52=0.3, 06:54=0.41, 06:56=0.28, 06:58=0.38, 07:00=0.31. There is no elevated slow-query regime during or after onset, so query latency did not step before or with the connection growth.

user-db replication_lag_ms is flat ~27.6-32.3ms (mean 29.98, min 27.65, max 32.31) for every one-minute bucket 06:30-07:10, including 06:51=30.99, 06:52=30.47, 06:54=30.77, 06:56=31.55. No replica-lag/IO step precedes or coincides with the connection growth, so the DB's storage/replication layer shows no fault.

Comparison of onset timestamps: the user-db connection step is at ~06:52 UTC (F13's connection growth confirmed at one-minute resolution), while the auth-service traffic surge begins in the 06:47-06:48 bucket (F16: ~765 avg / 1425 max req/s vs ~391-404 before) and auth-service p99/503 onset is ~06:54. So the connection step (06:52) does NOT precede the traffic surge (06:47); it follows it by ~4-5 minutes and itself precedes only the worker-pool saturation (06:54:53).

user-db has no connection-wait / pool-saturation / query-latency metric beyond what was queried: its full available_metrics list is [connections_active, cpu_pct, disk_used_pct, replication_lag_ms, slow_queries_per_min]. There is no connection-wait or pool-saturation series to inspect, so query latency (slow_queries_per_min) and connections_active are the only proxies available for H4.

api-gateway request_rate rose from a flat ~1,180-1,325 req/s baseline through the 06:48 bucket to 4,790 req/s in the 06:58 bucket (~3.9x), i.e. the gateway itself sees the surge, in the same 120s buckets in which auth-service's rate rose. Values (avg): 06:48=1227.99, 06:50=1500.82, 06:52=2327.7, 06:54=3294.15, 06:56=3939.86, 06:58=4790.49 (max 4859.74).

auth-service request_rate rose on the identical bucket grid from a flat ~383-418 req/s baseline through 06:48 to avg 1749.75 (max 1813.74) at 06:58; the two services' surge onsets coincide (both first clearly above baseline in the 06:50 bucket: gateway 1500.82, auth-service 452.43), so the gateway is NOT flat while auth-service rises -- the pattern expected for an auth-service-only internal retry/loop is absent.

The gateway carries the larger absolute volume and a comparable multiplier (gateway ~3.8-3.9x and 4.8k vs auth-service ~4.5x and 1.75k req/s), i.e. auth-service's rate is a fraction (~37%) of the gateway's throughout, consistent with auth-service traffic being a subset of genuine gateway inbound traffic rather than a multiplied internal echo.

api-gateway shows no retry/loop, throttle or upstream-error log signature in 06:30-07:00: all 7 matched entries are INFO, the top pattern is 'connection pool stats: healthy' (4 occurrences, first 06:30:42), with 'config reloaded (no changes)' and a single 'served batch of requests, p50=473ms' at 06:50:25. No endpoint/client attribution lines exist.

The gateway's own error_rate stayed at baseline ~0.13-0.27% through the 06:51 bucket, then jumped to avg 6.23% (max 9.4) at 06:54 and 9.09% at 06:57 -- only ~half of auth-service's ~13.8-14.1% error rate -- indicating the 5xx failures originate at auth-service and are only partially reflected at the gateway, not generated at the gateway.

The api-gateway exposes no client/endpoint-level metric or log attribution for 06:30-07:00 (available_metrics are only cpu_pct, error_rate, latency_p99_ms, memory_pct, request_rate, restarts; the only log patterns are routine heartbeats), so the surge cannot be attributed to specific clients or to the /v1/auth/login endpoint from gateway telemetry.

findings.statement: api-gateway exposes NO client/IP-level, route/endpoint-level, retry, or upstream-5xx breakdown series. Four targeted queries all returned not_found with the same available_metrics list: request_rate_by_client ('service api-gateway has no metric request_rate_by_client'), request_rate_by_route (no metric request_rate_by_route), retries_per_sec (no metric retries_per_sec), upstream_5xx (no metric upstream_5xx). The gateway's complete metric set is only [cpu_pct, error_rate, latency_p99_ms, memory_pct, request_rate, restarts], so the decisive H1 test (single-client retry loop vs broad demand) cannot be answered from gateway metrics.

api-gateway's only surviving scalar rate series (request_rate) confirms a smooth, monotone ramp of genuine-looking traffic (not a single-step spike): 06:40-06:50 flat ~1178-1348 req/s, then 06:51 1652.95, 06:52 2164.64, 06:53 2490.76, 06:54 3174.6, 06:55 3413.7, 06:56 4002.1, 06:58 4721.24, rising through 07:04 5197.35 (26/26 points, missing_points 0). The growth builds across ~8 one-minute buckets rather than appearing as one instantaneous client-triggered jump.

api-gateway p99 latency steps from a flat ~201-226ms baseline (every bucket 06:40-06:53, e.g. 06:53 211.62) to 4024.51ms at 06:54 and stays 3648-4200ms through 07:05. This gateway-side latency step coincides exactly with auth-service's ~06:54 p99/503 onset (F8), i.e. the gateway's own latency is dominated by the slow auth dependency, not generated locally.

api-gateway logs at 06:40-07:05 contain ZERO error-level entries (ERROR query total_matched=0) and INFO-level logs show only routine patterns: total_matched 5, all INFO, top pattern 'connection pool stats: healthy' (4 occurrences, first 06:44:30) plus one 'served batch of requests, p50=473ms' at 06:50:25. There is no retry, throttle, upstream-5xx, or client-attribution log line anywhere in the window.

Combining gateway and auth-service rate series (F31/F32): gateway rises ~1.2k->~4.8-5.2k req/s (~4x) and auth-service ~400->~1.75k req/s (~4.5x) on the same minute grid with onset in the same 06:50-06:52 buckets. auth-service's rate is a stable ~37% fraction of the gateway's throughout (e.g. 06:58 gateway 4721.24 vs auth 1749.75), which is the shape of a subset of broadly-driven inbound traffic, not an internal amplified echo (which would show auth-service equal to or exceeding gateway).

Cross-service sweep 06:30-07:10 UTC (120s buckets, partial=false, 41/41 points): the three peer services on the api-gateway ingress show NO traffic step at 06:47-06:52. pricing-engine request_rate is flat 587-687 req/s (mean 644.23; 06:46=628.64, 06:48=663.71, 06:50=657.33, 06:52=645.5, 06:54=673.48) and market-data-service is flat 864-1025 req/s (mean 944.96; 06:46=944.59, 06:48=935.39, 06:50=969.07, 06:52=968.92, 06:54=996.16). Neither peer shows any onset in the 06:47-06:52 interval.

policy check: portfolio-service (the only deployer in the window, dep-5803 at 05:50) also shows no request-rate step: flat 523-618 req/s across 06:30-07:10 (mean 570.15; 06:46=558.9, 06:50=557.5, 06:52=572.61, 06:54=577.06, 06:58=591.38). So the portfolio-service co-tenant carries no surge either.

Peer latency_p99 is flat straight through the 06:47-06:54 onset window, i.e. no latency blast radius outside auth-service: pricing-engine p99 55.94-65.16ms (mean 59.79; 06:46=57.96, 06:50=58.48, 06:52=59.27, 06:54=58.18), market-data-service p99 35.67-42.56ms (mean 39.97; 06:46=40.67, 06:52=39.63, 06:54=39.02), portfolio-service p99 164.72-194.13ms (mean 180.32; 06:46=181.12, 06:52=179.62, 06:54=180.84). None steps at or before 06:47-06:52.

Peer error_rate (HTTP 5xx) is flat and low across the whole 06:30-07:10 window, with no step at 06:47-07:00: pricing-engine stays in 0.10-0.32% (mean 0.22; 06:48=0.23, 06:52=0.26, 06:54=0.24, 06:58=0.17) and market-data-service in 0.10-0.31% (mean 0.20; 06:48=0.18, 06:52=0.17, 06:54=0.26, 06:58=0.23). Neither peer degrades alongside auth-service's ~13.8-14.1% and the gateway's 6.23-9.09%.

Interpretation for blast radius: among the five services sharing the api-gateway ingress, the traffic step is present only on api-gateway (F31: ~1.18-1.33k -> 4.79k req/s) and auth-service (F12/F16/F32: ~391-404 -> ~1.5k req/s), both rising on the identical 120s bucket grid from the 06:50 bucket (gateway 1500.82, auth-service 452.43). pricing-engine, market-data-service and portfolio-service request_rate, latency_p99 and error_rate are all statistically indistinguishable from baseline across 06:47-06:52, so auth-service is the only downstream service that degrades and no peer shows onset at or before 06:47-06:52. The other four services receiving inbound traffic through the gateway are not affected.

Interpretation for the trigger question: because the peers' request_rate is flat while api-gateway and auth-service rise together on the same bucket grid, the 06:47-06:50 step is not visible as a platform-wide traffic step at any other ingress service, and it is not login-specific in its effect on volume (gateway total inbound rises ~3.9x, F31/F33). The evidence localises the surge to traffic entering through api-gateway and terminating at auth-service rather than being generated internally by auth-service, but does not identify which client/endpoint origin emitted it (F36: gateway has no client/endpoint attribution).
